description: Hello! We are high school seniors who are interested in space!
summary:
We built a website that helps mission planners and field-test teams choose where on Earth to rehearse the Moon and Mars. We compared 12 Earth sites with two targets: Malapert Massif, an Artemis candidate landing region near the Moon’s south pole, and Arcadia Planitia, a flat, ice-rich plain on Mars. Each condition (slope, maximum temperature, dust and highest Sun angle) is scored from 0 to 1 using NASA data (MODIS, LRO Diviner, MOLA, POWER), ESA’s Copernicus DEM and the LMD Mars dust climatology.

Our main finding is that no single site is best. Different sites win for different conditions, so we never combine scores into one ranking. Instead, the site shows which analog suits which test, and where Earth falls short: nowhere on Earth matches the Moon’s low Sun angle or extreme cold, or lunar and Martian gravity, vacuum and radiation.

Visitors can explore a map, compare sites, browse sites by mission task, spin 3D models of the Moon and Mars, and use a chat finder that recommends a site from a description like “hot and flat.” This matters because testing in the right place saves time and money before crews and rovers ever leave Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Analogs for Moon and Mars is a website that helps mission planners and field-test teams pick where on Earth to rehearse lunar and Martian missions. We compared 12 Earth sites with two targets, Malapert Massif on the Moon (an Artemis candidate landing region) and Arcadia Planitia on Mars. For each condition (slope, maximum temperature, dust and highest Sun angle), every site gets a score from 0 to 1 for how closely it matches the target. We never add the scores into one ranking, because the best site depends on which test you want to run.

Features
Visitors can explore a map, compare all sites, browse sites by mission task, and see where Earth falls short (for example, nowhere on Earth matches the Moon’s low Sun angle or extreme cold). A chat finder lets people describe what they need, like “hot and flat,” and links them to the best-matching site. A Mars/Moon Models page has 3D globes with NASA surface maps. Clicking a spot shows the most similar Earth site.

Benefits and impact
Testing in the right place saves time and money before crews, rovers and instruments leave Earth. Our results also show which test each site can support and where no Earth site can help.

Tools and data
We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for the 3D globes, Python for data processing, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Data comes from NASA MODIS, LRO Diviner, MOLA and POWER, ESA’s Copernicus DEM, and the LMD Mars dust climatology.

Creativity and factors considered
We kept each condition separate so people can see trade-offs instead of one hidden score. We also account for pixel size, so Earth and Mars slopes are compared at the same resolution, and we state where Earth can’t match the Moon or Mars.
